articles.title: Tamil Nadu: Anti-Corruption wing books senior DMK leader KN Nehru, associates over Rs 1,020 crore tender irregularities
articles.description: It is a setback for former DMK minister and senior leader K N Nehru after former ministers EV Velu and Senthil Balaji faced action over alleged corrupt deeds. The Directorate of Vigilance and Anti-Corruption (DVAC) has named K N Nehru and his two brothers among 13 persons as accused in a case concerning alleged manipulation of government tenders under the Municipal Administration, Urban and Water Supply (MAWS) department and the collection of illegal gratification disguised as “party fund”. The FIR alleges a wrongful gain of Rs 1,020 crore and states that illegal gratification was collected at 7.5%-10% of the contract value. 🚨 ED Document Proof- MAWS Dept scam 🚨 7.5 to 10 % – Party Fund Beneficiary – Stalin & Udhayanidhi.... 👀!!️ pic.twitter.com/ro8i41ajZo — Hari (@hari_noty) September 7, 2026 The others named in the FIR include Nehru’s brothers K N Manivannan and N Ravichandran, former Madhavaram DMK MLA S Sudarshanam, R K Nagar DMK MLA J J Ebenezer, TVH Group director Kavi Prasad, TVH managers D Ramesh and D Prabhu, besides other associates, contractors and government officials. The case relates to alleged manipulation of government tenders and collection of illegal gratification in contracts awarded between 2021 and 2025. The Directorate of Vigilance and Anti-Corruption (DVAC) has registered an FIR against former Municipal Administration Minister K N Nehru, his brothers, two sitting MLAs and senior municipal officials over an alleged Rs 1,020-crore tender manipulation and bribery scam. The FIR... pic.twitter.com/fLjqdn1DIJ — Rajalakshmi sampath (@Rajalakshmi2398) September 7, 2026 Acting on a complaint by the Enforcement Directorate (ED) Additional Director, DVAC registered an FIR against K N Nehru, his brothers K N Manivannan and N Ravichandran and others over alleged manipulation and corruption in MAWS contracts. Acting on a complaint by #ED Additional Director, #DVAC FIR against KN Nehru, his brothers KN Manivannan, N Ravichandran & others over alleged manipulation & corruption in Municipal Administration, Urban and Water Supply (MAWS) contracts.@xpresstn @NewIndianXpress @KN_NEHRU 1/7 pic.twitter.com/jkuTH8jP0o — S Mannar Mannan (@mannar_mannan) September 7, 2026 DVAC registered the case on September 4 following an inquiry based on the ED’s 258-page report on alleged irregularities in government contracts between 2021 and 2025. The FIR alleges that K N Nehru, named as the prime accused, facilitated access to senior IAS officers and influenced tender-awarding procedures. Also Read: Unmasking Stalin empire of corruption that tarnishes Tamil honour According to the FIR, Nehru’s brothers, K N Manivannan (A2) and N Ravichandran (A3), were accused of coordinating the collection and routing of illegal gratification. A calculation sheet recovered from Manivannan’s phone allegedly recorded receipts of Rs 11.982 crore and disbursements of Rs 11.669 crore, with a substantial portion allegedly passed on to him. The FIR further alleges that Nehru allowed his brothers to coordinate with his close associate Kavi Prasad to collect illegal gratification from contractors and public servants. The document states that Rs 1 crore was collected from V R Water Infra at Avinashi on Ravichandran’s directions. The FIR also cites other alleged V R Water Infra collections of Rs 2.77 crore, Rs 5 crore, Rs 2 crore and Rs 4 crore. One netizen claimed that the FIR against K N Nehru had already been decided in connection with the Madhavaram Booster tender for Rs 5.25 crore for a rainwater channel. The tender was opened on August 9, 2024, but was allegedly allotted or prefixed to a pre-decided bidder, with “party fund” or bribe allegedly collected. #DVAC #FIRமுன்னாள் அமைச்சர் நேரு அவர்கள் மீதான FIR,– முன்பே முடிவு செய்யப்பட்ட Madhavaram Booster ஒப்பந்தம் – 5.25கோடி மழைநீர் வாய்க்கால் ஒப்பந்தத்தில் – இலஞ்சம் (Party Fund)– ஒப்பந்தம் திறப்பு : 09.08.2024 ஆனால் யாருக்கு கொடுக்கவேண்டும் என 30.07.2024 இல் முடிவு(Pre Fixing) pic.twitter.com/kmpWvP3Ki2 — Rk (@comrade_rk) September 7, 2026 Kavi Prasad (A4), then director of True Value Homes (TVH) Group of Companies, allegedly acted as an intermediary by fixing meetings with officials, sharing tender information and helping “prefix” preferred bidders before tenders were opened. D Ramesh (A5) and D Prabhu (A6), also associated with the TVH Group, have been accused of handling collections in the Tiruppur and Coimbatore regions. R Sasipriya (A7), then Coimbatore town planning officer, is accused of collecting money from contractors and routing it to Manivannan through Ramesh and Prabhu. G Balachandran (A8) and G Murugesan (A9), then regional engineers in Tiruppur, are accused of facilitating municipal works and kickbacks. Former DMK MLAs Sudarshanam (A10) and Ebenezer (A11) are also accused of recommending contractors and sharing tender details and alleged bribe calculations with Prasad. The proprietor and office-bearers of C T Constructions in Chennai are named as A12, while contractor K Sathish Kumar is A13. The FIR also names unknown officials, contractors and firms. According to the FIR, the DVAC inquiry prima facie found a nexus between public servants, private individuals and contractors in the award of contracts. It alleged that contractors were identified even before tenders were opened and that illegal gratification was collected on the pretext of “party fund” at 7.5% to 10% of the contract value. Also Read: DMK government in Tamil Nadu ‘most corrupt’, committing atrocities against Hindus: Union Home Minister Amit Shah The FIR cites a WhatsApp exchange dated September 6, 2021, in which Sudarshanam allegedly sent Prasad details of a Chennai Metropolitan Water Supply and Sewerage Board (CMWSSB) tender. Against one item, “C&T 75 lakh” was written in blue ink, along with the contract value in pencil, which was sent 22 days before the tender was opened. One netizen said the ED document was reportedly leaked during the DMK government’s tenure itself and questioned why no arrests had been made in connection with the alleged scam. 🚨 CM Vijay – ED Document on MAWS Scam 🚨 The ED document as reportedly leaked during the DMK government’s tenure itself. !!️ 258-page ED document — TVK Govt completed 4 Months Not even a single person has been arrested in connection in this scam... 👀 https://t.co/Sl56aYi9J2 pic.twitter.com/5kazoP8HSI — Hari (@hari_noty) September 7, 2026 The issue stems from a report submitted by the ED on December 3, 2025. With the state government’s permission, the DVAC registered [...]

articles.title: India’s 6-Hour Solar-Storage Bet: How SECI Is Moving Beyond Daytime Solar
articles.description: With its latest 1,200 MW solar-plus-storage tender, SECI is procuring renewable power that can be delivered when the grid needs it most. The strong developer response and sharply lower tariffs point to a major shift in India’s renewable energy procurement strategy. For more than a decade, India’s solar story has largely been defined by scale and falling costs. The objective was straightforward: add as much low-cost solar generation as possible and bring down the cost of electricity. But as solar penetration increases, another challenge is becoming harder to ignore. Solar generation is abundant during the day, while some of the grid’s highest demand comes later in the day, when solar output begins to decline. This is where energy storage is increasingly becoming part of the solar procurement equation. The Solar Energy Corporation of India’s (SECI) latest tender for 1,200 MW of interstate transmission system (ISTS)-connected solar PV projects with 600 MW/3,600 MWh of energy storage systems (ESS) is a clear example of this transition. The projects have been awarded at tariffs of ₹3.12-3.13/kWh and are designed to provide firm and dispatchable renewable power rather than simply daytime solar generation. From cheap solar to firm power India’s move towards storage-backed renewable power did not begin with the latest SECI tender. One of the earliest major experiments came in 2020, when SECI conducted a 1,200 MW renewable energy tender requiring six hours of peak power supply. Greenko won 900 MW using pumped-hydro storage at around ₹6.12/kWh, while ReNew won 300 MW using battery energy storage at around ₹6.85/kWh. The latest tender therefore represents an important change in the economics of the model. Five to six years after that early six-hour procurement, successful bids have come in at just ₹3.12-3.13/kWh. The comparison is not completely like-for-like because the tender structures and market conditions are different. But the headline numbers nevertheless illustrate how dramatically the economics and competitiveness of storage-backed renewable power have evolved. SECI itself has continued to expand its procurement of renewable energy coupled with storage, including a 1,200 MW solar-plus-1,200 MWh ESS tender issued in 2024. Its subsequent tenders have increasingly focused on firm and dispatchable renewable energy rather than generation alone. What makes the latest tender different? SECI’s Tranche-XXI tender, issued in June 2025, sought 1,200 MW of ISTS-connected solar PV capacity along with 600 MW/3,600 MWh of ESS under a build-own-operate model. The headline number of 600 MW of storage capacity, however, does not tell the complete story. The tender requires at least 0.5 MW/3 MWh of ESS for every 1 MW of contracted project capacity. That translates into six hours of storage at the ESS's rated discharge capacity. In other words, the requirement is not simply to install batteries alongside a solar plant. The developer has to combine renewable generation and storage in a manner that allows the contracted power to be supplied during the hours specified by the buyer. The buyer can schedule six peak hours for drawing power from the storage system. The contracted energy requirement is 3 MWh for every 1 MW of project capacity across those hours. For the overall tender, that translates into 600 MW of ESS power capacity and 3,600 MWh of energy capacity. The six-hour requirement is really about the grid The significance of the tender lies less in the number six and more in what those six hours represent. Traditional solar projects sell generation when the sun is available. A storage-backed solar project, by contrast, is being asked to reshape that generation profile. The objective is to make renewable power available closer to the period when the grid needs it. This changes the commercial proposition for developers. They are no longer competing solely on the cost of solar generation. They have to optimise the combination of solar capacity, storage capacity, charging strategy, degradation, financing and power-delivery obligations. It also explains why the tender specifies penalties for shortfalls. Developers are responsible for meeting the contracted supply profile, with the applicable shortfall penalty going up to 1.5 times the tariff for electricity not supplied during the contracted period. The selected projects are also required to enter into 25-year power purchase agreements, giving developers a long-term revenue framework against which the substantial investment in generation and storage can be financed. Developers were clearly willing to compete The market response was significant. SECI received 24 bids representing an aggregate 6,150 MW against the 1,200 MW capacity on offer. That means the tender attracted more than five times the capacity being procured. Following technical and commercial evaluation, 23 bidders representing 6,060 MW were shortlisted for the electronic reverse auction. The result is particularly notable because the initial financial bids ranged from ₹3.40/kWh to ₹5.40/kWh, before competition through the reverse auction brought the winning tariffs down to ₹3.12-3.13/kWh. Interestingly, Oriana Power had bid for 300 MW but ultimately received 100 MW, while the other three successful bidders were awarded their full bid capacities. It is not necessarily a “BESS-only” story There is an important distinction in how the tender should be described. Although battery energy storage is likely to be a major technology for such projects, SECI’s requirement is for an energy storage system rather than exclusively a battery energy storage system. The tender is technology-agnostic, meaning developers can potentially use different commercially established storage technologies as long as they meet the contractual requirements. This is significant because six-hour storage sits at a point where technology selection becomes more consequential. Batteries can provide fast response and modular deployment, while longer-duration technologies such as pumped hydro can offer different economics and operational characteristics. The tender therefore represents a procurement requirement for a particular power-delivery profile rather than a government decision in favour of one storage technology.

articles.title: BHEL Leadership Reset Ahead of 2027: Why Succession Will Matter for India’s Power and Manufacturing Ecosystem
articles.description: Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited is approaching an important leadership inflection point. By the beginning of March 2027, India's public-sector engineering major could have a substantially different leadership team at the top. Chairman and Managing Director K Sadashiv Murthy is scheduled to superannuate on February 28, 2027, while Director Power Tajinder Gupta is also expected to retire on the same date. Director Engineering, Research and Development S M Ramanathan is scheduled to superannuate a month earlier, on January 31, 2027. With CMD K Sadashiv Murthy and two key functional directors approaching superannuation, BHEL faces one of its most significant management transitions in recent years. The timing is crucial: the engineering giant is carrying an order book of around ₹2.4 lakh crore and has returned to strong revenue and profit growth. Meanwhile, the position of Director Human Resources has remained vacant since March 2026, with Tajinder Gupta currently holding additional charge of the HR portfolio. On the surface, these may appear to be routine leadership changes associated with superannuation in a large Central Public Sector Enterprise. But the timing gives the developments much greater significance. BHEL is entering the transition at a moment when its business momentum, project pipeline, diversification strategy and role in India's energy security ambitions are all expanding simultaneously. The leadership change, therefore, is not simply about who occupies the corner office at BHEL House. It could influence how effectively one of India's largest engineering enterprises converts an enormous order pipeline into revenues, profitability, technological capability and opportunities for thousands of suppliers, contractors and MSMEs. A Major Transition at the Top K Sadashiv Murthy assumed charge as BHEL's Chairman and Managing Director on November 1, 2023. His present appointment runs up to February 28, 2027 or until further government orders. The Public Enterprises Selection Board process for identifying his successor has already been initiated, with the Ministry of Heavy Industries publishing the CMD vacancy in May 2026. Similarly, Tajinder Gupta, who joined BHEL's board as Director Power in September 2023, has emerged as an important operational leader during a period of renewed activity in India's thermal power sector. Following the departure of Krishna Kumar Thakur from the HR portfolio in March 2026, Gupta was also given additional responsibility as Director Human Resources. BHEL's official records confirm that Thakur relinquished charge on March 19, 2026 and Gupta subsequently assumed the additional HR responsibility. S M Ramanathan represents another strategically important position in the leadership structure. An IIT Madras-trained mechanical engineer with decades of experience across BHEL's manufacturing, engineering, R&D and operational ecosystem, Ramanathan assumed charge as Director Engineering, Research and Development on April 30, 2025. His experience spans hydro turbines, steam turbines, switchgear, digital technologies, production, project functions and finance. The near-simultaneous transition across CMD, Power, R&D and HR functions creates an unusual concentration of leadership change. That is what makes succession particularly important. Why the Timing Matters: BHEL Is Carrying a ₹2.4 Lakh Crore Order Book The leadership transition is taking place against a dramatically improved operating backdrop. BHEL reported turnover of approximately ₹32,350 crore for FY2025-26, representing growth of around 18 percent over the previous year. The company received orders worth approximately ₹75,000 crore during the year, taking its outstanding order book to roughly ₹2.4 lakh crore at the end of FY2025-26. Power-sector orders alone were worth approximately ₹59,000 crore, while around ₹16,000 crore came from industrial businesses including transportation, transmission, defence, process industries and industrial equipment. BHEL also commissioned or synchronised approximately 8.9 GW of power capacity during FY2025-26. These numbers fundamentally change the leadership discussion. For a company with such a large order book, the challenge is no longer confined to winning projects. The real test is execution . A ₹2.4 lakh crore order pipeline requires extensive coordination across engineering, procurement, manufacturing, project management, construction, vendors, logistics, working capital and customer interfaces. Any prolonged leadership vacuum across key operating functions could potentially slow decision-making at precisely the stage when execution velocity becomes critical. Conversely, a well-managed transition could allow the next leadership team to inherit one of the strongest opportunity pipelines BHEL has seen in years. Profitability Has Also Started Improving Another important factor is BHEL's improving financial performance. In the April-June quarter of FY2026-27, BHEL reported consolidated net profit of approximately ₹376.7 crore compared with a loss of around ₹455.5 crore during the corresponding quarter of the previous year. Revenue from operations increased more than 40 percent year-on-year to approximately ₹7,698 crore. Significantly, the company's power business returned to profitability during the quarter. Power-segment revenue grew to about ₹5,919.5 crore, compared with ₹3,898.9 crore during the corresponding period a year earlier. This means BHEL's next leadership is unlikely to inherit a company merely attempting a turnaround. It could inherit a company entering the execution phase of that turnaround . And these are very different management challenges. Winning orders requires competitiveness. Executing a massive backlog requires project discipline, supply-chain management, working-capital control and rapid decision-making. The Next CMD Will Have Five Strategic Priorities The incoming leadership will potentially need to simultaneously manage five major priorities. First will be order execution. The company's huge order book must translate into predictable revenue and cash flow. EPC execution, vendor coordination, project closures and timely delivery will remain critical. Second will be diversification beyond conventional power equipment. BHEL has been expanding capabilities across nuclear energy, defence, transportation, transmission, hydrogen, coal gasification and other emerging technologies. The company itself has stated that it is building capabilities in areas including defence, aerospace, urban mobility, rail transportation, hydrogen and carbon capture. Third will be technology. The retirement of the Director Engineering and R&D assumes significance because BHEL is simultaneously trying to strengthen indigenous technology capabilities. The company has recently pursued partnerships in areas such as electrolyser technologies while positioning itself for emerging opportunities associated with India's clean-energy transition. BHEL announced strategic tie-ups during 2026 relating to both alkaline and PEM electrolyser systems. Fourth will be people and organisational transformation. The HR director's position has already required an additional-charge arrangement. With several senior executives approaching superannuation, succession planning below board level will also become important. For an organisation with extensive engineering and manufacturing capabilities accumulated over decades, preserving institutional knowledge while bringing younger leadership into decision-making will be essential. Fifth will be supply-chain development. And this is where the transition becomes particularly relevant to India's MSME ecosystem. Why BHEL's Leadership Transition Matters to MSMEs BHEL is much more than a large PSU operating in isolation. Behind its power plants, industrial equipment and infrastructure projects exists a significant ecosystem of equipment manufacturers, fabricators, engineering firms, component suppliers, service providers, contractors and MSMEs. A growing BHEL order book can therefore produce a multiplier effect throughout Indian manufacturing. The company's procurement system actively engages suppliers across numerous manufacturing and project categories. BHEL also encourages MSME suppliers to register on TReDS platforms for receivables financing and operates centralised procurement arrangements for several project requirements. For MSMEs, three issues will consequently be important during the leadership transition: Continuity of procurement: Large project pipelines require predictable tendering and purchase orders. Faster vendor payments: MSMEs supplying complex engineering projects depend heavily on timely cash flows. Vendor capability development: As BHEL enters higher-technology businesses such as nuclear, defence, hydrogen and advanced transmission, Indian SMEs will need support to meet increasingly sophisticated quality and certification requirements. This represents an opportunity. Instead of viewing vendors simply as suppliers, the next BHEL leadership could treat MSMEs as strategic manufacturing partners. Such an approach would strengthen both BHEL's execution capability and India's broader objective of creating deeper domestic manufacturing supply chains. Energy Security Makes BHEL Strategically Important BHEL's relevance also needs to be viewed within India's changing energy landscape. While renewable energy capacity is expanding rapidly, India's electricity requirement continues to grow. Thermal generation remains an important part of the country's energy security architecture, while nuclear power is expected to assume a larger role over the coming decades. BHEL is positioned across several parts of this transition. It retains a strong presence in thermal power equipment while simultaneously expanding into transmission, nuclear technologies, rail transportation, defence and new-energy technologies. Its own strategic outlook has identified nuclear energy as an important opportunity, especially as India works toward significantly expanding nuclear generation capacity over the longer term. The challenge for the next leadership will therefore not be to choose simply between conventional and clean energy. It will be to position BHEL across India's entire evolving energy architecture . Leadership Continuity Will Be Closely Watched The government and Public Enterprises Selection Board have already initiated processes relating to future leadership positions. The CMD vacancy was advertised during May 2026, while the post of Director Power was subsequently advertised in June. The Director HR vacancy had also been advertised earlier following the position becoming vacant in March. That advance planning becomes important because large engineering companies benefit from continuity. Strategic decisions made today can affect projects that will remain under execution for five or even ten years. Power plants, transmission systems, nuclear equipment and industrial projects do not operate according to quarterly timelines. They require institutional consistency. SMEStreet Perspective: This Is More Than a PSU Appointment Story The forthcoming leadership changes at BHEL should therefore not be viewed merely as another round of PSU appointments. They arrive at a defining stage for the company. BHEL has regained revenue momentum. Its order book has expanded dramatically. Its power business is showing signs of stronger financial performance. At the same time, the company is attempting to move deeper into new technology-led areas. The next CMD and functional directors will have to protect this momentum. The ultimate measure of success will not be the size of the order book inherited by the new leadership, but how effectively that order book gets converted into completed projects, revenues, profitability and stronger domestic manufacturing capabilities. For India's MSMEs, the transition carries another message. A stronger, faster and more technologically ambitious BHEL could become an even larger anchor customer for India's engineering SMEs, component manufacturers and industrial service providers. That makes leadership continuity at BHEL relevant not only to shareholders and policymakers but also to thousands of enterprises operating throughout India's industrial supply chain. As February 2027 approaches, the focus will naturally remain on who succeeds K Sadashiv Murthy and the other retiring directors. But the more important question will be what mandate the next leadership receives. If the mandate combines disciplined execution, technology development, supplier ecosystem expansion and aggressive diversification, BHEL's approaching leadership transition could mark not simply a change of guard — but the beginning of the company's next growth cycle.
